title: JLPT or EJU: Which One Your Target Actually Requires
summary: These are not two grades of one exam. Which you need depends on what you apply to — and some places use a minimum score as an eligibility condition.
body_html:
Students often treat these as a ladder — JLPT first, EJU if you are serious. They are not a ladder. They test different things and they are used differently by different kinds of institution.

Getting this wrong costs a test cycle, which in practice means a term.

They test different things

The EJU, and university entrance exams generally, require the ability to answer questions on the basic subjects you studied up to high school — in Japanese. [source:1]

Read that twice. It is not a Japanese exam with harder vocabulary. It is your school subjects, asked in Japanese. Someone with strong Japanese and weak mathematics is not ready for it, and someone with strong mathematics is still stuck if they cannot read the question.

This is why a school running a university-preparation course teaches the basic subjects alongside the language. [source:1] At one such school the course covers EJU, JLPT and entrance exam preparation together, with teachers who combine subject expertise with experience teaching non-native speakers. [source:1]

Who uses which

The division is real and it follows the type of institution.

Universities. The required subjects for the EJU and the JLPT level sought differ by institution and by faculty. [source:1] Some universities set an EJU minimum score as a condition of eligibility to apply. [source:1]

That last point is the one that catches people. An eligibility condition is not a selection factor you can offset with a strong application — fall below it and you cannot apply at all.

Vocational schools. Some set a JLPT pass level, specifically N2 or N3, or an EJU minimum score, as an eligibility condition. [source:1]

So for vocational schools the JLPT route genuinely exists as an alternative. For universities, the EJU is doing work the JLPT does not do — because the EJU reports subject scores and the JLPT does not.

What this means for your sequence

Work from the target backwards, which is the opposite of how most people do it.

If you are aiming at a specific university faculty, find its required EJU subjects and any minimum score before you choose which subjects to study. [source:1] Requirements differ by faculty within the same university. [source:1] Choosing subjects first and checking requirements later is how people end up with scores in the wrong subjects.

If you are aiming at vocational school, find out whether your target accepts JLPT and at what level. [source:1] If N2 is the bar, that is a different preparation plan — and a different timetable — from an EJU plan. [source:1]

If you do not know yet, prepare for the EJU. It is the harder requirement and it keeps both doors open. The reverse is not true: a JLPT level does not substitute for a subject score.

The two things neither exam covers

Both of these decide outcomes and neither is a test score.

The statement of purpose. Most universities and vocational schools require one at application. [source:1] It has to say why that school and why that field, convincingly, and in a way only you could have written. [source:1]

The interview. You convey your motivation verbally, and what is being assessed is not only your reasons — it is whether your listening and speaking are good enough to follow classes after admission. [source:1]

So a candidate with a good EJU score and no practice at speaking is exposed at exactly the point where nothing can be revised.

And a separate exam you may already need

Do not confuse any of this with the Japanese-ability evidence now required at the visa stage. That is a different requirement, at a different point in your application, and it is verified in a different way. Its standard is set by the immigration agency, not by any school, and it is covered separately below.

Clearing it tells you nothing about being ready for the EJU. They are not on the same scale and they are not for the same purpose.

Before you book anything

  • Identify the specific institution and faculty, not the type of school. Requirements differ by faculty. [source:1]
  • Check whether there is a minimum score used as an eligibility condition rather than as a selection factor. [source:1]
  • For vocational school, check whether JLPT is accepted and at what level — N2 and N3 are both in use. [source:1]
  • If undecided, prepare for the EJU. It covers more ground and the JLPT does not substitute for it.
  • Start the statement of purpose early. It is required by most institutions and it cannot be produced in a week. [source:1]
  • Practise speaking even if your target weights the written exam. The interview tests whether you can follow classes. [source:1]

If your prior schooling is shorter than Japan requires, no exam score fixes that — see do you actually qualify for a Japanese university and the designated preparatory course explained. For the visa-stage Japanese requirement, which is separate from both exams, see how that requirement is verified. For a school whose courses are built around these exams, see the Sendagaya group comparison.

Exam requirements are set by each receiving institution and change by admission year. Confirm them on the institution's own admissions page for the year you are applying for — the school page linked below describes how the requirements work, not what any particular university requires of you.

claims_without_sources: EJU と JLPT の試験科目・配点・実施時期・受験料 —— 実施主体（日本学生支援機構・国際交流基金等）の一次資料を本記事では引いておらず、学校ページの記述の範囲（どちらがどう使われるか）に限定した。試験そのものの仕様を書くなら実施主体を出典にする必要がある。
「迷っているなら EJU を準備せよ」という推奨 —— 出典のある事実（大学は EJU の基準点を出願資格に用いることがある／専門学校は JLPT でも可）からの当方の結論であって、学校の推奨ではない。
N2・N3 がどの程度の日本語力かという説明 —— JLPT の水準定義は国際交流基金の管轄で、本記事の出典にはない。レベル名のみ引いた。
ビザ段階の A1 要件と EJU の難易度関係 —— 「同じ尺度ではない」とだけ述べた。両者を比較する公的な対応表は存在しない。
大学・専門学校ごとの具体的な基準点 —— 各校の募集要項の管轄。本記事では一切挙げず、「志望校の募集要項で確認せよ」とした。
ビザ段階の日本語要件の具体的な水準（参照枠の A1 相当）—— 出典は入管庁の通知であり、本記事の出典域（校方官網）外。ここで水準を書くと学校ページを出典として示したことになるため落とし、専用記事へのリンクに委ねた。闸门が未標記の数字として弾いたのが正しい。
